parsed.study_design: IRB-approved cross-sectional Rapid Assessment Process study
parsed.population_and_sample: Eleven recipient communities (six rural, four peri-urban, and one urban) with recently completed water-supply interventions, plus twelve government, intergovernmental, and NGO officials; community interviews included men and women and prioritized village leaders, water committee members, ritual water specialists, and other residents.
parsed.exposure: Recently completed government- or externally supported water-supply interventions and their governance arrangements, including community participation, prior needs assessment, integrated WASH programming, water-user groups, local operation/maintenance/repair capacity, institutional coordination, and consultation with traditional water specialists.
parsed.outcome: Water-service availability, reliability, and sustainability, including population served, seasonal variation, local maintenance capacity, user-group support, and perceived changes in health, education, economic status, water-fetching distance, and time spent on chores.
parsed.rationale: The Methodology section (pp. 166-168) identifies an empirical cross-sectional RAP covering eleven communities and agency officials, using interviews, observation, focus groups, social-network analysis, and simple statistical tests. Tables 1-2 and the Survey Findings (pp. 168-170) report service and access-related outcomes after water-source interventions, including people served, seasonal functioning, maintenance capacity, and reduced water-fetching burden. The study also directly examines governance and administrative mechanisms—needs assessments, user groups, community participation, traditional authority, and inter-agency coordination—linked to project functioning and sustainability (Discussion, pp. 170-171).
